passage: Saturday. Found Papa's old torch in the drawer that doesn't work. I asked Keerthana didi if I could open it. She said yes, but first took the battery out and gave me the small screwdriver from her box. Inside there was a spring, a tiny round bulb and a metal strip! I pressed the strip and the spring pushed back. My heart went boom. I took out everything and put it on the table in a line. Then I could not put it back. The spring jumped away twice. Keerthana didi found it under the cupboard. We put it together, and on the third try the light came on. I clapped. Arohi

qa.q: What did Keerthana didi do before letting Arohi open the torch?
qa.a: She took the battery out and gave Arohi the small screwdriver from her box.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when pressing the strip and seeing the spring push back?
qa.a: Arohi felt thrilled and full of curiosity, and the heart went boom.

qa.q: How did Keerthana didi make the tinkering safe and useful?
qa.a: She took out the battery first, lent a small screwdriver and helped find the lost spring, so the torch could be put back together.

qa.q: What might Keerthana didi think when the spring jumped away twice?
qa.a: She was probably patient and amused, ready to help find the spring, since she wanted Arohi to keep exploring.

grounding: Shows a child taking apart an old torch to see inside, thrilled but unable to put it back without safe help.

passage: The alarm clock in Binita's house in the village had stopped years ago and lay on the shelf like a dead beetle. On Sunday, her older brother Eshaan gave her a small screwdriver and a plate. "Unscrew only the back, and put every screw on the plate." Binita worked slowly. Inside were wheels with tiny teeth and a coiled spring. She turned one wheel with her finger, and another wheel moved. "They're holding hands!" she whispered. When she tried to close it again, the wheels would not line up. Dada came and showed her where the small wheel fitted. The clock ticked for a minute. Binita listened with her head on her arm.

qa.q: What did Eshaan tell Binita to put on the plate?
qa.a: Eshaan told Binita to put every screw on the plate.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she said "They're holding hands!"?
qa.a: Binita felt amazed and delighted at seeing how one wheel moves another.

qa.q: What helped Binita understand the clock even though she could not put it back alone?
qa.a: Eshaan gave her a small screwdriver and a plate, and Dada showed where the small wheel fitted.

qa.q: How might Dada feel when helping Binita fit the wheel?
qa.a: Dada is probably pleased and patient, glad that Binita is curious about how things work.

grounding: Shows a child taking apart an old clock to see inside, thrilled and unable to put it back alone, with safe supervised tools.

passage: In their Hyderabad flat, Aditi, nine, found an old torch in the drawer. It didn't work. She sat on the balcony floor and unscrewed the top. A spring jumped out. Then a tiny bulb. Then the batteries. She lined up the pieces on a newspaper, eyes shining. "So the spring pushes the battery to touch the bulb!" But when she tried to put it back together, the spring wouldn't fit. Her uncle, Kiran chacha, came out with his toolbox. "Want to see how the switch works?" He handed her a small screwdriver and showed her how to hold it. Together they cleaned a rusty metal strip. The torch lit up. Aditi squealed.

qa.q: What did Aditi find in the drawer?
qa.a: An old torch.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling as she lined up the pieces?
qa.a: She felt excited and curious, her eyes shining as she worked out how the spring pushed the battery.

qa.q: How did Kiran chacha help Aditi learn from her tinkering?
qa.a: He gave her a small screwdriver, showed her how to hold it and worked with her to fix the switch.

qa.q: How might Kiran chacha feel when the torch lit up?
qa.a: Kiran chacha likely felt pleased and proud, sharing Aditi's joy at getting it to work.

grounding: Shows a child taking apart an old torch with delight, unable to reassemble it until an adult offers safe tools and guidance.

passage:
Harsha: "Zeenat! What happened to the alarm clock?"
Zeenat: "I opened it, Abbu. I wanted to see what makes it tick."
Harsha: (looking at the pieces on the bed) "And?"
Zeenat: "There are little wheels with teeth! When one turns, the next turns. It's like a chain!"
Harsha: "Can you put it back?"
Zeenat: "...No. There's one wheel left over."
Harsha: (sitting down) "You know, I did the same with my father's radio."
Zeenat: "Were you in trouble?"
Harsha: "Big trouble. So here's a deal. On Sundays, you and I open one old thing together. With the right screwdrivers. And you draw where each piece goes before you take it out."
Zeenat: "Can we start with the old fan?"
Harsha: "Unplugged. Yes."

qa.q: What did Zeenat take apart?
qa.a: The alarm clock.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel about what she found inside?
qa.a: Zeenat felt excited and fascinated by the little wheels with teeth, even though one was left over.

qa.q: Why is Harsha's Sunday deal a good response?
qa.a: It turns curiosity into supervised learning with the right tools, and drawing each piece first helps Zeenat put things back.

qa.q: How does Harsha see Zeenat's tinkering?
qa.a: Harsha sees himself in it, remembering his father's radio, and chooses to guide rather than scold.

grounding: A dialogue shows a child thrilled by taking apart a clock that won't go back together, and a parent offering supervised tinkering.

passage: I'm Rafiq, and when I was ten, I took apart my toy car to find out why it zoomed when you pulled it back. My friend Tejas watched while I used a butter knife to pry off the bottom. Inside was a coiled spring and tiny gears, like a secret city. I shouted so loudly that Ammi came running. I couldn't get it back together, and the car never zoomed again. I was sad for about ten minutes. Then Ammi's brother, who fixes bicycles, gave me a small screwdriver set and said I could use it only at his shop, with him beside me. Every Saturday after that I took something apart there. I still remember the feeling of that first coiled spring.

qa.q: What did Rafiq use to pry off the bottom of the car?
qa.a: A butter knife.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel on seeing the spring and gears?
qa.a: Rafiq felt thrilled and amazed, shouting so loudly that Ammi came running.

qa.q: What made Ammi's brother's gift a wise one?
qa.a: The screwdriver set came with supervision at his shop, which turned curiosity into safe, useful tinkering.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt watching the car come apart?
qa.a: Tejas probably felt curious and excited too, and maybe a little worried when it wouldn't go back together.

grounding: A young adult recalls taking apart a toy car with delight as a child and being given supervised access to proper tools.

passage:
After-school care note, Thursday.
Maria found the broken wind-up car in the toy box and asked to "see its insides". I gave her a small screwdriver and a tray. She took out four tiny screws, lifted the shell and gasped. "It's all little wheels with teeth!" She turned the key and watched the gears spin, laughing. Then she pulled the spring out, and it uncoiled with a ping across the table. Nothing would fit back after that. Her face crumpled. The car was broken anyway, so I asked what the spring had been doing. "It pushes the teeth wheels round." Next week I'll bring an old kitchen timer, and Irawati from the older group will show her how to photograph each step so things can go back.

qa.q: How many screws did Maria take out of the car?
qa.a: Four tiny screws.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when she lifted the shell, and then when nothing fitted back?
qa.a: She was delighted and amazed at the "wheels with teeth", then briefly upset and disappointed when the spring flew out and it wouldn't go back together.

qa.q: What did the care worker do that made the tinkering useful?
qa.a: Gave her a proper small screwdriver and a tray, stayed with her, and asked what the spring had been doing, turning the mess into understanding.

qa.q: How might Irawati's photo idea help Maria next time?
qa.a: Photographing each step gives Maria a record of the order, so her curiosity can end with the object back together instead of in pieces.

grounding: Shows a child who opens an old toy to see how it works, is thrilled by the gears but can't reassemble it, and gains from supervised tinkering with safe tools.
